To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the human interferon-alpha genes are arranged in seven linkage groups, that the genes within each group are related by a common evolutionary origin, that the individual genes differ in the degree of sequence divergence, and that at least some of the genes are related by gene conversion events.

the human IFN-alpha locus is a complex locus comprising at least seven linkage groups, that the number of functional genes in the locus is not known with certainty, but may be as low as 12 and that the total number of IFN-alpha-related genes, including pseudogenes, is at least 23.
the human IFN-alpha gene family comprises 23 loci (15 functional genes, six pseudogenes, and two unsequenced loci) and at least 18 allelic sequences.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of human IFN-alpha-related genes and their pseudogenes.
the molecular characterization of the human IFN-alpha gene cluster, and with the structural relationship of the genes and pseudogeness within this cluster.
the structural relationship between the IFN-alpha-related genes, pseudogenes and their flanking sequences.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
at least 20 distinct IFN-alpha genes exist in the human genome.

the IFN-alpha genes are organized in at least seven linkage groups, and that there are 23 distinct loci, 15 of which are likely to encode functional proteins, and eight of which may be allelic to these.
there are 15 potentially functional IFN-alpha genes and 9 pseudogenes in the human genome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the IFN-alpha locus is a complex region of the human genome, containing multiple genes, pseudogenes, and allelic variants, which are dispersed among seven linkage groups.
the human genome contains 23 IFN-alpha locii, 15 of which are potentially functional genes.
, at present, we know the complete nucleotide sequence of at least one gene for each of the seven linkage groups, and we know of 15 additional potentially functional loci.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the IFN-alpha locus appears to have been subjected to a complex history of gene duplication and gene conversion, and that this locus is likely to be the result of the evolution of a single ancestral IFN-alpha gene.

the human IFN-alpha genes have evolved from a limited number of primordial genes, and that the IFN-alpha gene family is much less complex than previously thought.
